# Scope and main finding

This report reconstructs the **hypothetical trial in Table 2**, not the
paper's simulation tables. It uses the patient-level toxicity outcomes
printed in the paper and **computes the doses from the appendix rules**.
The expected doses are a separate reference file; they are never passed to
the decision engine.

The replay matches **all 45 dose assignments**, all 30 continuation Go
decisions, all 15 final exits, and the week-56 completion. It reproduces all
nine final dose/cycle count cells. There is one apparent typo among the
63 printed cumulative count cells: at week 40, cycle 3 D2, the patient rows
give **1/3**, whereas the printed total is **1/6**.

Three files contain the statistical functions: `R/mtpi2.R`, `R/basyc.R`, and
`R/mts.R`. The short helper file handles report formatting and independent
reference comparisons. The design code uses **base R only**. Knitting this
report needs `rmarkdown` and `knitr`.

Use the shared `phase1-dose-finding.Rproj` in the parent folder. This exercise
has no separate R project or render helper. From the shared project root,
run `rmarkdown::render("Lyu_2018/reproduce_table2.Rmd")` or
`source("Lyu_2018/validate.R")`; from this folder, use
`rmarkdown::render("reproduce_table2.Rmd")` or `source("validate.R")`.
All generated tables stay in this exercise's `results/` folder.

The primary source is Lyu, Curran and Ji (2018),
[DOI 10.1200/PO.18.00020](https://doi.org/10.1200/PO.18.00020):
Figure 2 on p. 5; Table 2 on pp. 6-8; appendix on pp. 16-18.

# The appendix rules in executable form

## Independent beta-binomial working models

Let $d$ index dose and $j$ index cycle. For each dose/cycle cell, accumulate
**all observed outcomes at that cell**, across cohorts:

$$
x_{dj}\mid n_{dj},p_{dj}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_{dj},p_{dj}),
\qquad p_{dj}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1),
$$

$$
p_{dj}\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1+x_{dj},1+n_{dj}-x_{dj}),
\qquad r_{dj}=\Pr(p_{dj}>p_T\mid D).
$$

These are working models for trial decisions. They do not fit a parametric
longitudinal toxicity or carryover model. The final sequence TPC calculation
is a separate step.

```{r settings}
settings <- basyc_settings(n_dose = 3, target = 0.30,
                           ei = c(0.25, 0.35), xi = 0.95)
settings
```

## The reusable mTPI-2 module

The equivalence interval is $(0.25,0.35)$. Split the lower and upper tails
into intervals of width 0.10, truncating only the intervals at 0 and 1.
For each interval $I$, compute

$$
\operatorname{UPM}(I)=\frac{\Pr(p\in I\mid x,n)}{|I|}.
$$

The interval with the largest UPM gives E (below the EI), S (in the EI), or
D (above the EI). The posterior overdose rule adds DU when $r>0.95$.
The code evaluates the **same small module separately at different
dose/cycle cells**. It never merges the current-cycle and next-cycle counts.

```{r mtpi2-examples}
mtpi2_intervals(settings$ei)

examples <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 3), n = c(3, 3, 6))
examples$decision <- mapply(mtpi2_decision, examples$x, examples$n,
                            MoreArgs = list(settings = settings))
knitr::kable(examples, caption = "Three mTPI-2 decisions used in the replay")

# Inspect every interval's posterior mass and UPM for 1 DLT in 3 patients.
knitr::kable(mtpi2_scores(1, 3, settings), digits = 5)
```

For zero observations the implementation returns S. Exact UPM ties prefer
D, then S, then E. These explicit conventions do not affect Table 2.

## Continuation and safety

For a cohort completing cycle $j<J$, DCR examines the lowest dose in the
**destination cycle**:

$$
\mathrm{DCR}(j)=
\begin{cases}
\mathrm{NG},&r_{1,j+1}>\xi,\\
\mathrm{G},&r_{1,j+1}\le\xi.
\end{cases}
$$

Patients exit after the last cycle. Additionally, the trial stops when any
cycle's lowest dose satisfies $r_{1j}>\xi$. If dose $d$ in cycle $j$ is unsafe,
exclude all $(d',j')$ with $d'\ge d$ and $j'\ge j$, permanently. Global trial
stopping takes precedence over further continuation or allocation.

## DAR-1, DAR-2a and DAR-2b

Write $T(d,j)$ for the candidate dose index returned by the cell-specific
mTPI-2 module, bounded to the available dose range.

- **Default:** cohort 1 receives D1 in every cycle, subject to continuation.
- **DAR-1:** a new cohort's cycle-1 dose is $T(d_{\mathrm{previous}},1)$,
  using the preceding cohort's cycle-1 dose and cumulative cell data.
- For an existing patient moving from $j$ to $j+1$, set $i_1=T(d,j)$.
  If the previous cohort used several doses in cycle $j+1$, calculate all
  their candidates and take

$$
i_2=\min_{u\in\{\text{previous cohort's doses in cycle }j+1\}}T(u,j+1).
$$

Then use the current patient's observed toxicity $Y$:

$$
d_{\mathrm{next}}=
\begin{cases}
\min(i_1,i_2),&Y=0\quad\text{(DAR-2a)},\\
\min\{\max(d-1,1),i_2\},&Y=1\quad\text{(DAR-2b)}.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus, after a DLT at D1, the patient can remain at D1 if continuation is
allowed. A DLT does not automatically remove an individual from all later
cycles: the motivating trial assumes washout and recovery.

`dar2()` handles each patient separately using the same rule. This preserves
the personalized split: patients sharing a dose and current outcome receive
the same decision. All distinct doses used by the previous cohort are
included in $i_2$ even when that cohort has split into subcohorts.

# Reconstruct Table 2 from outcomes

## Read only the toxicity inputs

The CSV codes O as 0 and X as 1. Dose paths are not in this input file.

```{r input}
input <- read.csv(lyu_path("data", "table2_outcomes.csv"))
knitr::kable(input, caption = "Patient-level outcomes transcribed from Table 2")
outcomes <- as.matrix(input[, c("y1", "y2", "y3")])
```

## Run the design

At each eight-week epoch, the engine observes **all outcomes due at that
time**, updates cumulative counts and safety, then makes allocation
decisions. It enrolls a new cohort after the preceding cohort finishes
cycle 1. The preceding cohort's destination-cycle outcomes are observed
before being used in DAR-2. No future outcome is used.

```{r replay}
fit <- run_basyc(outcomes, cohort_size = 3, cycle_weeks = 8,
                 settings = settings)
data.frame(Patients = fit$n_patient, Observed_patient_cycles = nrow(fit$observed),
           End_week = fit$end_week, Stopped_early = fit$stopped)
```

## Compare all computed doses with the publication

Only now read the separate expected-dose fixture. Every assigned dose was
already calculated above.

```{r dose-comparison}
dose_check <- compare_table2_doses(fit)
stopifnot(nrow(dose_check) == 45, all(dose_check$match))
knitr::kable(dose_check, caption = "45 computed doses versus the independent Table 2 transcription")
```

## Inspect the split at week 16

The cycle-1 D2 data are 1/3, giving candidate D2; the destination cycle-2
D1 data are 0/3, also giving candidate D2. Patients 5-6 therefore receive
D2. Patient 4 experienced a DLT, so DAR-2b lowers that patient's dose to D1.

```{r week16}
knitr::kable(subset(fit$assignments, week == 16 & cohort == 2,
                    select = c(patient, cycle, rule, current, i1, i2, dose)))
```

## Inspect the previous cohort's split at week 24

Cohort 2 used D1 and D2 in cycle 2. Both modules contribute to cohort 3's
destination-cycle candidate: D1 has 0/4 and suggests D2, but D2 has 1/2 and
suggests D1. Their minimum is D1. Current cycle-1 D2 also has 3/6 and
suggests D1. All three patients in cohort 3 receive D1 in cycle 2.

```{r week24}
knitr::kable(subset(fit$assignments, week == 24 & cohort == 3,
                    select = c(patient, rule, current, previous, i1, i2, dose)))
```

# Table 2, assessment by assessment

The following panels preserve the patient-level information in Table 2,
using a compact layout. **O/X at D# is observed; Assigned D# is a planned
next cycle whose outcome is not available yet.** Historical completed
patients are left as individual rows instead of being compressed with an
asterisk. The count rows contain observed patients only.

```{r weekly-panels, results='asis', echo=TRUE}
for (week in seq(8, 56, by = 8)) {
  cat("\n\n## Week ", week, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(table2_at_week(fit, week), format = "html",
                     table.attr = "class='table table-condensed'"))
  cat("\n\n")
  s <- fit$snapshots[[as.character(week)]]
  cells <- matrix(paste0(s$x, "/", s$n), nrow = settings$n_dose)
  count_table <- data.frame(Cycle = seq_len(fit$n_cycle), t(cells), check.names = FALSE)
  names(count_table)[-1] <- paste0("D", seq_len(settings$n_dose))
  print(knitr::kable(count_table, format = "html",
                     table.attr = "class='table table-condensed'",
                     caption = "Cumulative DLTs / observed patients"))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

At week 48, patients 13-15 have finished cycle 2 and are assigned cycle-3
doses D1, D2, D2. At week 56 their outcomes are X, X, O, respectively.
This changes cycle-3 D1 from 1/6 to 2/7 and D2 from 2/6 to 3/8.

# Publication discrepancies, kept visible

## Table 2's week-40 denominator

```{r printed-count-check}
total_check <- compare_table2_totals(fit)
data.frame(Count_cells = nrow(total_check), Matching = sum(total_check$match),
           Discrepancies = sum(!total_check$match))
knitr::kable(subset(total_check, !match))
```

At week 40, only patients 7-9 have completed cycle 3 at D2, with one DLT.
Patients 10-12 are **assigned** D2 at that visit; their cycle-3 outcomes
arrive at week 48. Consequently, 1/3 is the patient-level total at week 40.
The printed 1/6 apparently counts patients who have not yet completed that
cycle. We retain the printed value in the reference CSV but do not use it
to corrupt the observed-data counts. This difference does not change the
Table 2 allocations, because DAR-2's minimum still yields D2.

## Figure 2 versus the unqualified appendix safety rule

The appendix says to exclude when $\Pr(p>0.30\mid x,n)>0.95$ without a
minimum $n$. For $(x,n)=(2,2)$:

$$
p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(3,1),
\qquad \Pr(p>0.30\mid D)=1-0.30^3=0.973.
$$

Thus the appendix gives NG/DU. Figure 2 instead shows G/D. Requiring at
least three patients for the safety override reproduces the printed
figure, but that requirement is not explicitly in the appendix.

```{r figure2-check}
reference <- figure2_reference()
appendix_table <- decision_tables(settings = settings)
figure_settings <- basyc_settings(safety_min_n = 3)
figure_table <- decision_tables(settings = figure_settings)
different <- reference$DAR != appendix_table$DAR |
             reference$DCR != appendix_table$DCR
knitr::kable(data.frame(reference[different, ],
                        Appendix_DAR = appendix_table$DAR[different],
                        Appendix_DCR = appendix_table$DCR[different]))
stopifnot(all(reference$DAR == figure_table$DAR),
          all(reference$DCR == figure_table$DCR))

# Both conventions give the same 45 doses in Table 2.
figure_fit <- run_basyc(outcomes, settings = figure_settings)
stopifnot(all(compare_table2_doses(figure_fit)$match))
```

```{r figure2, fig.width=12, fig.height=6, fig.cap='Printed-Figure-2 convention: minimum n=3 for the safety override. All 135 cells in each panel match the independent transcription.'}
plot_decision_tables(figure_table)
```

# Final MTS: an explicit implementation of Appendix p. 18

## Sequence-specific data and posterior screening

Retain completed, actually used sequences that pass the posterior safety
screen. For sequence $s$, use only patients completing that sequence:

$$
\widetilde q_s=\frac{\sum_j x_{sj}}{\sum_j n_{sj}}.
$$

This differs from averaging the pooled dose/cycle empirical rates used
during allocation. The appendix's screen uses **any** unsafe cycle
($\exists j$), despite an inconsistent use of the word "each" in its prose.

```{r sequence-data}
knitr::kable(sequence_summary(fit), digits = 4)
```

## Orderings, PAVA and votes

Order by intensity $I(s)=\sum_jd_{sj}$. Enumerate all permutations within
each tied intensity group; for this dataset there are $2!\times3!=12$
complete orderings. Apply PAVA over **each full ordering**, including
violations between different intensities.

```{r pava-demo}
# A violation between positions 2 and 3 is pooled, without changing ranks.
pava(c(0.10, 0.30, 0.20, 0.40))
```

For each ordering $w$, select a sequence nearest to $p_T$. Count its
selection frequency over orderings. Only at the final vote stage restrict
to nonincreasing dose sequences, then choose the most frequent one. Final
frequency ties favor lower intensity, then lower first, second, ... dose.

The appendix does not fully specify **PAVA weights** or **nearest-target
ties inside an ordering**. Therefore these arguments are required, and we
show sensitivity rather than claiming a unique published MTS for Table 2.

```{r mts}
mts <- select_mts(fit, weights = "equal", nearest_tie = "lower")
knitr::kable(mts$per_order)
knitr::kable(mts$votes)
mts$recommendation
```

```{r mts-sensitivity}
choices <- expand.grid(weights = c("equal", "patient_cycles"),
                        nearest_tie = c("lower", "higher"),
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
choices$MTS <- mapply(function(w, t) {
  select_mts(fit, weights = w, nearest_tie = t)$recommendation
}, choices$weights, choices$nearest_tie)
knitr::kable(choices)
```

Here the within-ordering tie convention changes the recommendation from
(2,1,1) to (2,2,1). **Table 2 does not report a final MTS**, so these choices
cannot be adjudicated against a published Table 2 recommendation. If no
nonincreasing sequence receives a vote, the implementation returns no MTS
instead of silently introducing another fallback rule. Enumeration stops
with an informative error if it would exceed `max_orders`.

# Checks, reuse and saved results

The validation includes independent Table 2 and Figure 2 transcriptions,
absence of future-outcome leakage, early stopping, permanent upper-dose /
later-cycle exclusion, dose boundaries, the first-cohort default and PAVA
pooling. It writes detailed audit CSVs to `results/`.

```{r validation}
# The script prints a console summary; show the same results once as a table.
invisible(capture.output(source(lyu_path("validate.R"), echo = FALSE)))
knitr::kable(checks, caption = "Executable validation checks")
```

To replay another outcome matrix with the same regular enrollment calendar,
replace `outcomes` and run `run_basyc()` again. The input has one row per
patient and one column per cycle; the number of patients must be a multiple
of the cohort size. A replacement mTPI-2 module can be supplied through
`decision_fun`, with signature `function(x, n, settings)` returning E/S/D/DU.
BaSyc's separate DCR and trial-wide safety rules remain active.

This replay assumes equal cycle durations, no additional dropout or recovery
delays, and one new cohort each cycle while accrual is open. A general
calendar with delayed outcomes would need an explicit waiting-event
implementation. Changing outcomes in the input is a programming exercise;
an operating-characteristic simulation additionally needs a specified
toxicity-generating model under adaptively assigned doses.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```

# References

Lyu J, Curran E, Ji Y (2018). Bayesian Adaptive Design for Finding the Maximum
Tolerated Sequence of Doses in Multicycle Dose-Finding Clinical Trials.
*JCO Precision Oncology* 2:1-19.
[DOI: 10.1200/PO.18.00020](https://doi.org/10.1200/PO.18.00020).

Guo W, Wang SJ, Yang S, Lynn H, Ji Y (2017). A Bayesian interval dose-finding
design addressing Ockham's razor: mTPI-2. *Contemporary Clinical Trials*
58:23-33. [DOI: 10.1016/j.cct.2017.04.006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cct.2017.04.006).

Separate implementation reference:
[R documentation for lrstat::mTPI2Table](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/lrstat/html/mTPI2Table.html).
The local mTPI-2 code uses the beta-binomial interval calculation directly;
it does not require this external package.
